decks.title: Business Services, Part 1: Banking and E-banking
goals: Describe the characteristics of business services
Distinguish commercial, cooperative, specialised and central banks
Explain the functions of commercial banks, including deposits and lending
Explain e-banking channels and payment systems as of 2024, with benefits and risks

slides.heading: Business Services: Banking
slides.body_md: Part 1: **banks**, their **functions** and **e-banking**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: business services, types of banks, functions of banks, e-banking, benefits and risks
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Imagine Farida, who runs a small shop and needs a place to keep her takings, a way to pay suppliers and some borrowing when stock runs short. A bank gives her all of these. In this part we study the types of banks, what a commercial bank does, and how electronic banking works, as of two thousand twenty four.

slides.heading: What makes a service different
slides.body_md: A **business service** is an activity that gives the customer a benefit without any physical product changing hands.

rows: Cannot be touched; there is no stock to hold
Produced and used at the same moment
The customer takes part in the process

visual.alt: Table of the characteristics of business services: intangible, inseparable and needing customer involvement, with examples such as banking, insurance, post and warehousing

slides.narration: Services are intangible, so there is no stock to keep on a shelf. They are inseparable, because they are produced and used at the same moment. And the customer usually takes part in the process. Banking, insurance, post and warehousing are all examples, and this chapter studies them one by one.

slides.heading: Types of banks
slides.body_md: Banks differ in who owns them and whom they serve.

visual.caption: Four groups of banks; commercial banks have three kinds.

slides.narration: This tree shows four groups of banks. Commercial banks take deposits and lend, and they are public sector, private sector or foreign. Cooperative banks are owned by their members. Specialised banks serve one sector, such as foreign trade, agriculture or small industry. At the top of the system stands the central bank.

slides.heading: Commercial banks
slides.body_md: A **commercial bank** accepts deposits from the public and lends them to earn a return.

rows: Head office abroad; works through branches here

visual.alt: Table of commercial banks: public sector, private sector and foreign banks with their main idea

slides.narration: In a public sector bank, the government holds the major stake. A private sector bank is owned by private shareholders. A foreign bank has its head office in another country and works through branches here. All three do the same basic work of taking deposits and giving loans, and all are supervised by the central bank.

slides.heading: Cooperative, specialised and central banks
bullets: Cooperative banks are owned by members.
Specialised banks serve one sector, for example foreign trade.
The Reserve Bank of India is the central bank.

rows: Owned by members; helps farmers and small borrowers
One sector: foreign trade, agriculture, small industry
Banker to the government and to banks; regulator

visual.alt: Table of cooperative, specialised and central banks with their roles

slides.narration: A cooperative bank is owned by its members and helps farmers and small borrowers. A specialised bank serves one sector, for example an export import bank for foreign trade or a rural development bank. The Reserve Bank of India, the central bank, is banker to the government and to other banks, and it regulates the banking system.

slides.body_md: Weavers who own a bank together.

visual.caption: Five functions around the commercial bank.

slides.narration: A commercial bank performs five functions. It accepts deposits and it lends. It offers cheques and other payment instruments, and it helps remit funds from place to place. And it provides allied services, such as lockers, bill payment and collection of cheques. We take each function in turn.

slides.heading: Accepting deposits
bullets: Current: for traders
Savings: for households
Fixed and recurring: for planned saving

rows: Traders; many transactions; usually no interest
Lump sum kept for a fixed period

visual.alt: Table of four kinds of deposit accounts: current, savings, fixed and recurring, with who uses them and how

slides.narration: A current deposit is for traders who deal often, and it usually pays no interest. A savings deposit is for households, pays interest and usually limits withdrawals. A fixed deposit keeps a lump sum for a fixed term. A recurring deposit collects a fixed instalment every month. Choose by looking at how the money will be used.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which deposit?
slides.body_md: Match four imagined customers to the best account.
bullets: Step 1: Note how often money moves.
Step 2: Note whether it is a lump sum or a monthly amount.
Step 3: Name the account and give a reason.

rows: Rs 2,000 every month for 12 months, Rs 24,000 in all
One big sum idle for two years

visual.alt: Worked example table matching four imagined customers to deposit accounts: shopkeeper to current, clerk to recurring, dentist to fixed and student to savings
visual.caption: Match the need to the account.

slides.narration: Farida deals every day, so she needs a current account. Salma saves a fixed amount every month, so she needs a recurring deposit, which collects twenty four thousand rupees over twelve months before interest. Isha has a big idle sum for two years, which suits a fixed deposit. Ravi saves small amounts, so a savings account fits.

slides.heading: Lending
bullets: Overdraft: beyond the balance, up to a limit
Cash credit: against stock
Loan: one sum, repaid in instalments

rows: Pay out more than the balance, up to a limit
Draw as needed against stock, up to a limit
One sum for a purpose, repaid in instalments
Cash now for a bill due later, less a deduction

visual.alt: Table of four lending facilities: overdraft, cash credit, loans and advances, and discounting of bills of exchange

slides.narration: An overdraft lets an account holder pay out more than the balance, up to a limit, and interest is charged only on the amount overdrawn. Cash credit lets a business draw as needed against its stock. A loan gives one sum for a purpose, repaid in instalments. Discounting turns a bill that is due later into cash today.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: overdraft and discounting
slides.body_md: Two imagined businesses use their banks.
bullets: Step 1: Overdrawn amount is the cheques minus the balance.
Step 2: Compare it with the limit.
Step 3: A discounted bill pays face value minus the deduction.

rows: Rs 35,000 overdrawn, within the limit of Rs 50,000

visual.alt: Worked example table: cheques of forty-five thousand against a balance of ten thousand give thirty-five thousand overdrawn within a limit of fifty thousand; a bill of one lakh twenty thousand discounted with a deduction of three thousand gives one lakh seventeen thousand today
visual.caption: Imagined figures.

slides.narration: Taruni Stores has ten thousand rupees and issues cheques worth forty five thousand. So thirty five thousand is overdrawn, which is within its limit of fifty thousand. Separately, a bill for one lakh twenty thousand is discounted, with a deduction of three thousand, so the bank pays one lakh seventeen thousand today.

slides.heading: Quick check: lending facilities
slides.body_md: Match each borrowing arrangement with its facility.
slides.narration: For each case ask how the money is drawn: beyond the balance, against stock, in one sum, or against a bill not yet due.

slides.heading: Cheques, remittance and allied services
bullets: Cheques and drafts replace cash.
Transfers move money between places.
Lockers and bill payment are allied services.

rows: Order to the bank to pay a sum from the account
Bank-issued order for payment at another place
Money moved between accounts or places

visual.alt: Table of payment instruments and allied services: cheque, bank draft, transfer, locker, bill payment and collection of cheques

slides.narration: A cheque is an order to the bank to pay a sum from the account, and a bank draft is a payment order issued by the bank itself. Remittance means moving money from one place to another, by draft or by transfer. Allied services include lockers for valuables, payment of bills and collection of cheques.

slides.heading: E-banking: meaning and channels
slides.body_md: **E-banking** means banking through electronic channels, as of 2024.

rows: Use the bank's website to check accounts, pay and transfer
Do the same through the bank's app on a phone
Cash and other services at any hour
Spends the bank's money; the holder repays later

visual.alt: Table of e-banking channels as of 2024: internet banking, mobile banking, automated teller machine, debit card and credit card

slides.narration: E-banking is banking through electronic channels. As of two thousand twenty four, the main channels are internet banking and mobile banking, the automated teller machine, and debit and credit cards. A debit card spends the balance of the holder, while a credit card spends money lent by the bank, which the holder must repay later.

slides.narration: Follow a payment from a customer to a supplier. The customer sends an instruction with a secret code. The bank of the customer checks it and debits the account. The payment system carries the message. The bank of the supplier credits the account, and a confirmation returns. Different systems differ in how fast and in what amounts they work.

slides.body_md: Arrange the steps of an electronic fund transfer.
slides.narration: Start with the customer and end with the supplier bank. The payment system sits in between.

slides.heading: Transfer systems, as of 2024
bullets: Learn the idea of each system, as of 2024
Rates, charges and limits change; do not quote them

rows: Each payment settled at once; for large amounts
Instant app payment from a linked bank account; launched 2016

visual.alt: Table of electronic transfer systems as of 2024: batch-wise National Electronic Funds Transfer, real time gross settlement for large amounts, immediate payment service for instant transfer, and the unified payments interface launched in 2016

slides.narration: As of two thousand twenty four, National Electronic Funds Transfer settles payments in batches. Real time gross settlement settles each payment at once and is meant for large amounts. Immediate payment service gives instant transfer between accounts. The unified payments interface, launched in two thousand sixteen, gives instant payment through a mobile app linked to a bank account.

slides.heading: Debit and credit cards
bullets: Debit card: own money, deducted at once
Credit card: bank money, repaid later

visual.alt: Table comparing a debit card and a credit card on whose money is used, when the account is affected and the nature of each

slides.narration: Both cards are used at shops and machines, but they differ in whose money is used. With a debit card the amount is taken from the balance of the holder at once. With a credit card the bank lends the money and the holder repays later. So a credit card is both a payment tool and short term credit.

slides.heading: Benefits and risks of e-banking
bullets: Benefits: access at any hour, lower cost, records, less cash
Risks: fraud; never share codes

visual.alt: Table of the benefits and risks of e-banking: access at any hour, lower cost, a record of transactions and less cash handling against fraud, stolen passwords, shared one time passwords and the need for security habits

slides.narration: E-banking offers access at any hour, lower cost, convenience, a record of every transaction and less cash handling. Its risks are fraud and the need for security. Keep your personal identification number and passwords secret, never share the one time password, and log in only through the official app or website.

slides.heading: What insurance is
slides.body_md: **Insurance** is a contract in which the insurer agrees, for a premium, to compensate the insured for a loss from a stated risk, or to pay a sum on a life event.

slides.narration: Insurance is a contract. The insurer agrees, in return for a premium, to compensate the insured for a loss from a stated risk, or to pay a sum when a life event occurs. It works by pooling risk: many people pay small premiums, and the few who suffer a loss are paid from the common fund.

slides.narration: Seven principles guide insurance contracts. Utmost good faith, insurable interest, indemnity, proximate cause, subrogation, contribution and mitigation of loss. Not every principle applies to every policy. In particular, indemnity does not apply to life insurance. We now see each one in an imagined case.

slides.heading: Good faith, interest and mitigation
bullets: Disclose every material fact
No financial stake means no valid policy

rows: Kamlesh hides a heart ailment; the insurer may refuse the claim
A stranger cannot insure a neighbour's shop; the owner can
After a fire, the owner saves the unburnt stock and calls the fire service

visual.alt: Table of three principles with imagined cases: utmost good faith, insurable interest and mitigation of loss

slides.narration: Under utmost good faith, the proposer must reveal every material fact, so hiding a heart ailment lets the insurer refuse the claim. Insurable interest means a financial stake in the subject, so a stranger cannot insure the shop of a neighbour. Under mitigation of loss, the insured must try to limit the damage, for example by calling the fire service.

slides.heading: Indemnity and proximate cause
bullets: Indemnity: actual loss, no profit
Proximate cause: must be an insured risk

rows: Compensation is the actual loss, up to the sum insured; not applied to life insurance
The nearest effective cause must be an insured risk
A fire policy pays for fire, not for a flood

visual.alt: Table of indemnity and proximate cause: compensation limited to actual loss, the nearest effective cause must be insured, and a fire policy pays for fire and not flood

slides.narration: Indemnity means the insured is brought back to the earlier position but is not allowed to gain. Compensation is the actual loss, up to the sum insured. Proximate cause means the nearest effective cause of the loss must be an insured risk. So a policy against fire pays for fire but not for a flood.

slides.heading: Subrogation and contribution
bullets: Subrogation: the insurer recovers from the party at fault
Contribution: insurers share in proportion to cover

rows: After paying, the insurer takes over the insured's right to recover from the party at fault
When two policies cover one risk, insurers share the loss in proportion to their cover

visual.alt: Table of subrogation and contribution with their rules

slides.narration: Subrogation lets an insurer, after paying the claim, step into the shoes of the insured and recover from the party who caused the loss, so the insured cannot gain twice. Contribution applies when two policies cover one risk. The insurers then share the loss in proportion to the amounts they cover.

sections.body_md:
A business service is intangible, cannot be separated from its production and needs the customer to take part. Banking, insurance, post, warehousing and transport are examples.

**Types of banks:** commercial banks (public sector, private sector, foreign); cooperative banks; specialised banks (for example an export-import bank, a rural development bank, a small industry bank); and the central bank, the Reserve Bank of India, which is banker to the government and to banks and the regulator of the banking system.

A bank that accepts deposits from the public and lends them to earn a return.

sections.heading: 2. Functions of commercial banks
sections.body_md:
**Deposits:** current (traders, many transactions), savings (households), fixed or term (lump sum for a period), recurring (monthly instalment).

**Lending:** overdraft (pay beyond the balance up to a limit), cash credit (draw against stock up to a limit), loans and advances (one sum, repaid in instalments), discounting of bills of exchange (cash today for a bill due later, less a deduction).

**Cheques and payment instruments; remittance** of funds by drafts and transfers; **allied services** such as lockers, bill payment and collection of cheques.

key_terms.definition_md: A facility to withdraw more than the balance, up to an agreed limit.
A limit sanctioned against stock or goods from which the borrower draws as needed.
Paying the holder of a bill of exchange its value less a deduction before the due date.

sections.heading: 3. E-banking (as of 2024)
sections.body_md:
E-banking is banking through electronic channels. The systems below are dated as of 2024; rates, charges, limits and timings change, so learn the idea, not a figure.

**Channels:** internet banking, mobile banking, automated teller machines, debit cards, credit cards.

**Transfer systems:** National Electronic Funds Transfer (batch-wise), real time gross settlement (each payment settled at once, for large amounts), immediate payment service (instant transfer), unified payments interface (instant payment through a mobile app; launched 2016).

**Benefits:** access at any hour, lower cost, convenience, a record of transactions, less cash handling. **Risks:** fraud; keep codes secret and never share a one time password.

key_terms.definition_md: Banking through electronic channels such as the internet, mobile apps, machines and cards.
A card that spends the holder's own bank balance.
A card that spends the bank's money, to be repaid by the holder later.

sections.heading: 4. Insurance and its principles
sections.body_md:
Insurance is a contract in which the insurer agrees, for a premium, to compensate the insured for a loss from a stated risk, or to pay a sum on a life event. It works by pooling the risk of many.

**Principles:** utmost good faith (disclose every material fact); insurable interest (a financial stake in the subject); indemnity (compensation up to the actual loss, no profit; not for life insurance); proximate cause (the nearest effective cause must be an insured risk); subrogation (the insurer who has paid recovers from the party at fault); contribution (insurers sharing a loss in proportion to cover); mitigation of loss (the insured must act to limit the damage).

key_terms.definition_md: The price paid to the insurer for the cover.
Compensation that restores the insured to the earlier position, without profit.
The insurer taking over the insured person's right to recover from the party at fault.

sections.body_md:
**Postal services (as of 2024):** financial services (postal savings schemes, money transfer) and mail services (parcel, registered post, speed post, insured post). **Courier services:** private, door-to-door, fast, with tracking.

**Warehousing:** storing goods from production until needed. **Types:** private, public, bonded (imported goods awaiting customs duty), government, cooperative.

**Functions:** consolidation, break-bulk, stockpiling, value-added services (packing, grading), price stabilisation, and financing (a warehouse receipt is security for a loan).

key_terms.definition_md: Storing goods from the time of production until they are needed.
A licensed warehouse holding imported goods until customs duty is paid.
A document showing goods stored, which a lender can accept as security.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Quoting rates, charges, limits or timings for payment systems; describe the idea and add as of 2024.
- Mixing overdraft with cash credit, or a debit card with a credit card.
- Applying indemnity to life insurance.
- Mixing the time at which insurable interest is needed.
- Treating a bonded warehouse as free of duty; the duty is postponed.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a correct option or a quoted line from the case.
- 2 and 3 marks: one point per feature or function with a short explanation.
- 5 marks: five points, each with an explanation, in a numbered list.
- Case questions: quote the line, name the concept, explain in a sentence.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a business service such as banking?

options.text_md: It cannot be touched or held, so it is intangible
It can be produced in advance and kept in stock until a customer arrives
It is produced and consumed at the same time, so the two cannot be separated
The customer usually has to take part in the process

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It can be produced in advance and kept in stock until a customer arrives. A service cannot be stored, so the first statement is the one that does not fit. Intangibility, inseparability of production and consumption, and customer involvement are all standard characteristics.

questions.stem_md: Westmark Bank, an imagined institution with its head office abroad, opens three branches in imagined Ranipur to serve companies and traders. In which group of commercial banks does it fall?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Foreign banks. A commercial bank whose head office is outside the country but which works through branches here is a foreign bank. Public sector banks are those where the government holds the majority stake, private sector banks are owned by private shareholders based in the country, and cooperative banks are owned by their members.

questions.stem_md: Seventy handloom weavers of imagined Pushpagiri set up their own bank. Each weaver is a member and part-owner, the bank lends mainly to members, and surplus is meant to serve them. This is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** cooperative bank. A bank owned and run by its members for their benefit is a cooperative bank. A specialised bank serves one sector such as foreign trade, a foreign bank has its head office abroad, and the central bank regulates the whole system rather than lending to weavers.

questions.stem_md: Bharat Niryat Bank, an imagined institution, exists only to give finance and guidance to firms that sell goods abroad. It is best described as a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** specialised bank. A bank set up to serve one sector, here foreign trade, is a specialised bank. A commercial bank takes deposits from the public for general lending, a cooperative bank is member-owned, and the central bank is the country's top monetary authority.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the Reserve Bank of India, as the central bank, is correct?

options.text_md: It competes with commercial banks for the savings accounts of households
It lends only to farmers and small industry
It acts as banker to the government and to other banks, and regulates the banking system
It is owned by the customers of cooperative banks

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It acts as banker to the government and to other banks, and regulates the banking system. The central bank keeps the government's accounts, holds the accounts of other banks and supervises them. It does not compete for household savings, it is not confined to one sector, and its ownership is not with cooperative bank customers.

questions.stem_md: Farida Khan, an imagined shopkeeper in imagined Nilgiri Nagar, deposits her day's takings and writes several cheques to suppliers every week. Which deposit account suits her purpose best?

options.text_md: Savings account meant for a household

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Current account. A business with frequent deposits and withdrawals suits a current account, which has no tight cap on transactions. A fixed deposit locks money for a term, a recurring deposit collects fixed monthly instalments, and a household savings account limits frequent business withdrawals.

questions.stem_md: Salma Jacob, an imagined clerk, puts Rs 2,000 into her bank every month for 12 months to build a fund for her daughter's fees. This is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** recurring deposit. Fixed monthly instalments over a chosen period are the mark of a recurring deposit, which after 12 months holds Rs 24,000 of her own money plus interest. A fixed deposit is one lump sum, a current account serves traders, and an overdraft is a borrowing facility.

questions.stem_md: Taruni Stores, an imagined business, has Rs 10,000 in its current account and an overdraft limit of Rs 50,000 agreed with its bank. It issues cheques worth Rs 45,000. How much is overdrawn, and is it within the limit?

options.text_md: Nothing is overdrawn, because cheques cannot exceed the balance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Rs 35,000, within the limit. The overdrawn amount is the cheques minus the balance, that is 45,000 minus 10,000, which is 35,000, and that is below the limit of 50,000. Rs 15,000 is the room still left, not the overdrawn amount, and an overdraft facility exists precisely to allow payment beyond the balance.

questions.stem_md: Surya Fabrics, an imagined seller, holds a bill of exchange for Rs 1,20,000 that falls due in two months. It hands the bill to its bank, which pays Rs 1,17,000 at once and collects the full amount from the buyer on the due date. This service is called

options.text_md: discounting of a bill of exchange

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** discounting of a bill of exchange. The bank pays the bill's value less a deduction (Rs 3,000 here) before the due date, which is discounting. A fixed deposit and a draft involve different flows of money, and a locker is a safekeeping service.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, which description fits National Electronic Funds Transfer?

options.text_md: Every payment is settled one at a time in real time, meant for large amounts
Transfers are collected and settled in batches rather than one by one
It is a card that draws on the holder's own balance
It is a mobile app that links to a virtual payment address

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Transfers are collected and settled in batches rather than one by one. Batch-wise settlement is the feature of this system. Individual real-time settlement for large amounts describes real time gross settlement, a card drawing on the balance is a debit card, and a virtual payment address belongs to the unified payments interface.

questions.stem_md: A builder in imagined Kasturi Nagar must send a very large payment to a steel supplier and wants each payment settled individually, with no waiting for a batch. As of 2024, which channel is meant for this?

options.text_md: A debit card at a shop counter

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Real time gross settlement. Real time gross settlement is the system designed for large-value payments settled one by one. A debit card suits shop purchases, a recurring deposit is a savings product and a cheque collection takes more time and is not real time.

questions.stem_md: Meghna Das, an imagined college student, pays a canteen owner by scanning a code on her phone, using an app linked to her bank account, and the money moves within moments. As of 2024, which system is she using?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Unified payments interface. A phone app linked to a bank account for instant payment is the unified payments interface, launched in two thousand sixteen. Real time gross settlement is for large amounts, a draft is a paper instrument, and a credit card uses borrowed credit rather than the bank balance.

questions.stem_md: Pavan Joshi, an imagined traveller, buys a bag using a plastic card and the amount is taken straight from his own savings balance. He is using a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** debit card. A debit card draws on the holder's own balance, so the money leaves the account at once. A credit card is a loan from the bank that the holder repays later, and a draft and a locker key are not payment cards.

questions.stem_md: A caller claiming to be from imagined Nilgiri Mercantile Bank asks Rohan Iyer for the one time password just sent to his phone, to stop a block on his account. The sensible response is to

options.text_md: give it quickly so that the account is not blocked
share it only if the caller knows his name
refuse and never share it, because a bank does not need the password from the customer
share it, then change his personal identification number

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** refuse and never share it, because a bank does not need the password from the customer. A one time password is a secret meant only for the customer's own transaction, and genuine staff never ask for it. Giving it away, even to someone who knows personal details, allows a fraudster to complete a transfer before any later change can help.

questions.stem_md: While buying a life policy, Kamlesh Rao, an imagined applicant, hides the fact that he has had a serious heart ailment. Years later the insurer finds out. Which principle has been broken?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Utmost good faith. The applicant must disclose every material fact, and hiding a heart ailment breaks utmost good faith, so the insurer can refuse the claim. Subrogation concerns recovery from third parties, contribution concerns sharing among insurers, and indemnity concerns the amount of compensation.

questions.stem_md: Pooja Hegde, an imagined tenant, wants to insure the shop of a neighbour in imagined Ranipur against fire, though she has no connection with it. Her policy would fail for lack of
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** insurable interest. She would not suffer a financial loss if the shop burnt, so she has no insurable interest, which is needed to make the contract valid. The other principles apply only once a valid policy and a loss exist.

questions.stem_md: Anand Foods Storage, an imagined firm, insured its stock against fire for Rs 5,00,000. A fire destroys stock whose real value was Rs 3,50,000. On the principle of indemnity, the insurer pays

options.text_md: nothing, because indemnity is not part of fire insurance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Rs 3,50,000, the actual loss. Indemnity means putting the insured back where he was, no better, so compensation is limited to the actual loss, which is below the sum insured. Paying the whole sum or a bonus would give a profit, and indemnity is in fact the basis of a fire policy.

questions.stem_md: An imagined godown in Ranipur is insured against fire only. A flood washes goods away, and the policy is then claimed. The insurer refuses because, under the principle of proximate cause,

options.text_md: any loss must be reported within a day
flood and fire are always the same peril
the insured failed to give notice of a second policy
the nearest effective cause of the loss was flood, which is not an insured risk

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the nearest effective cause of the loss was flood, which is not an insured risk. The effective cause decides the claim; the policy covers fire and the real cause here was flood. The other statements either invent a rule, wrongly equate two perils or refer to something that never happened in the case.

questions.stem_md: An imagined insurer pays Rs 4,00,000 for a shop damaged by a contractor's carelessness, and then recovers Rs 4,00,000 from the contractor. This follows the principle of
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** subrogation. After paying, the insurer steps into the shoes of the insured and recovers from the party at fault, so the insured cannot profit twice. The other three principles deal with disclosure, financial stake and the duty to limit damage.

questions.stem_md: Same stock, two policies: an imagined insurer A covers Rs 3,00,000 and an imagined insurer B covers Rs 2,00,000. A loss of Rs 2,50,000 occurs. Under the principle of contribution, how is it shared?

options.text_md: A pays Rs 2,50,000 and B pays nothing
A pays Rs 1,50,000 and B pays Rs 1,00,000
B pays Rs 1,50,000 and A pays Rs 1,00,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A pays Rs 1,50,000 and B pays Rs 1,00,000. The insurers share in the ratio of the sums they cover, 3 to 2, which gives Rs 1,50,000 and Rs 1,00,000. Paying twice would let the insured profit, and reversing the figures ignores the ratio.

questions.stem_md: Ishwar Menon, an imagined father in imagined Nilgiri Nagar, buys a policy so that his two young daughters receive a lump sum when they reach college age. This kind of life policy is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** children's policy. A policy aimed at funding a child's future needs is a children's policy. A joint life policy covers two lives together, an annuity pays regular amounts, and a whole life policy pays on death without a fixed term.

questions.stem_md: Orion Spices, an imagined exporter, owns the cargo loaded on an imagined ship when a storm sinks it. Under marine insurance, its insurable interest must be present

options.text_md: at the time of the loss
only at the time of buying the policy
neither at purchase nor at loss
only after the claim is paid

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** at the time of the loss. For marine policies the insurable interest must exist when the loss occurs, and Orion owned the cargo then. Requiring it only at purchase describes life insurance, and a claim paid before the interest exists makes no sense.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, which body regulates and promotes the development of the insurance business in India?

options.text_md: Securities and Exchange Board of India
Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. The authority named first was set up for exactly this purpose. The securities regulator looks after the securities market, the Registrar handles company registration and the small industries corporation supports small enterprises.

questions.stem_md: Leela Prasad, an imagined seller of pickles in imagined Ranipur, wants proof that her parcel was delivered and wants it to travel faster than ordinary post. As of 2024, which kind of mail service in general suits this?

options.text_md: Speed post with a tracking record

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Speed post with a tracking record. Speed post is a faster mail service that gives a record of delivery. An ordinary letter is slower, a savings scheme is a postal financial service and a locker is a bank service.

questions.stem_md: A boutique owner in imagined Kasturi Nagar wants a dress delivered right to a buyer's door the next day, with the parcel tracked on a phone. Which service is the natural choice?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A private courier service. Private courier firms specialise in fast door-to-door delivery with tracking. A bonded warehouse stores goods awaiting customs duty, a cooperative bank is a financial body and a savings scheme is a financial service.

questions.stem_md: Rangoli Imports, an imagined firm, brings machine parts from abroad but does not wish to pay customs duty until it knows how many parts it will sell. Where can the goods wait in the meantime?

options.text_md: A private warehouse owned by a competitor

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A bonded warehouse. A bonded warehouse is licensed to hold imported goods until the duty is paid. A competitor's private warehouse would not be bonded, a cooperative warehouse serves its farmer members, and a bank locker is for valuables.

questions.stem_md: Gita Mehra, an imagined small grain trader, has no storage of her own and rents space in a licensed warehouse that is open to anyone for a fee. Her warehouse is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** public warehouse. A warehouse open to all on payment of charges is a public warehouse. A private warehouse belongs to a firm for its own goods, a bonded warehouse holds goods pending duty and a cooperative one is owned by a society for its members.

questions.stem_md: Harvest Mart, an imagined buyer, stores onions in a warehouse during the plentiful season and releases them when the market is short, so that prices do not swing sharply. Which warehousing function is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Price stabilisation. Releasing stock when supply is short and holding it when supply is plentiful evens out prices. Consolidation joins small lots into one, break-bulk splits a large lot into small ones, and a value-added service such as grading changes the goods.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A commercial bank is able to give loans to businesses and households.

**Reason (R):** A commercial bank accepts deposits from the public.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. The money that depositors place with the bank is the main fund from which it lends, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** As of 2024, real time gross settlement is meant for payments of large amounts.

**Reason (R):** Each payment under this system is settled individually, in real time, rather than in a batch.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Because every payment is settled on its own without waiting, it is suitable where large sums need prompt, final settlement; R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A life insurance policy is a contract of indemnity.

**Reason (R):** The sum payable under a life policy is fixed in advance and does not depend on the measured value of a loss.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: a human life cannot be valued in money, so life insurance is a contract of guarantee, not indemnity. R is true and in fact shows why indemnity does not apply.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A fire insurer must pay for any loss to the stock, whatever the cause.

**Reason (R):** In fire insurance, fire must be the proximate cause of the loss.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: only losses whose proximate cause is the insured peril, fire, are covered. R is true and is exactly the rule that limits the insurer's liability.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Warehouses help to even out the prices of seasonal goods.

**Reason (R):** A warehouse receipt can be offered to a lender as security for a loan.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true. Price stabilisation arises from releasing stock at the right time, whereas the receipt's use as security is the separate financing function; R does not explain A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** E-banking can lower the cost of providing a service for a bank.

**Reason (R):** A customer must visit a branch for every transaction made through e-banking.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true because many transactions can be handled without branch staff or paper. R is false: the point of e-banking is that the customer can act through electronic channels without visiting a branch.

questions.stem_md: A life insurance policy is a contract of indemnity in which the insurer repays only the exact loss suffered.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Life insurance is a contract of guarantee: the sum is fixed in advance because the value of a human life cannot be measured.

questions.stem_md: In marine insurance, the insured must have an insurable interest in the subject matter at the time the loss occurs.
questions.solution_md: **True.** That is the rule for marine policies; it is not required at the time the policy is taken.

questions.stem_md: It is safe to tell a caller the one time password sent to your phone if he says that he is a bank employee.
questions.solution_md: **False.** A bank never needs the customer's one time password, so sharing it invites fraud.

questions.stem_md: A bonded warehouse holds imported goods until the customs duty on them has been paid or the goods have been re-exported.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Duty becomes due when the goods are released for sale at home; re-exported goods generally leave without home-market duty, as of 2024.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between a current deposit account and a savings deposit account.
questions.solution_md: Contrast on users, transactions and interest.

answer.model_answer_md: A current account is for traders and companies who make many deposits and withdrawals, and it usually pays no interest. A savings account is for individuals who want to save a little regularly, it pays interest and the number of withdrawals is usually restricted.

answer.model_answer_md: An overdraft lets a current account holder withdraw more than the balance up to an agreed limit, and interest is charged only on the amount overdrawn. questions.stem_md: A fire destroys goods of an insured trader worth Rs 3,50,000, while the policy is for Rs 5,00,000. Apply the principle of indemnity to say what the insurer pays.
questions.solution_md: State the principle and the amount.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three functions of a commercial bank.
questions.solution_md: Any three functions, each with a line.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Accepting deposits: it takes money from the public in current, savings, fixed and recurring accounts.
2. Lending: it gives overdrafts, cash credit and loans, and discounts bills of exchange.
3. Remittance of funds: it moves money between places through drafts and electronic transfers. Allied services such as lockers and bill payment are further functions.

questions.stem_md: State any three benefits of e-banking to customers.
questions.solution_md: Any three benefits.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Round-the-clock access: services can be used at any hour, so customers need not wait for branch hours.
2. Convenience and lower cost: payments and statements are managed from home, saving time and travel.
3. A record of transactions: every payment leaves an electronic trail, and less cash needs to be handled.

questions.stem_md: Meghna Das, an imagined customer, has started paying all her bills online. Explain three risks she faces and one way to reduce each.

3. Sharing the one time password with a fake caller: she should treat it as private and report suspicious calls to the bank.

questions.stem_md: Explain the three kinds of marine insurance, using an imagined shipping company, Sagar Lines, and an imagined exporter.

2. Cargo insurance: the exporter insures the goods loaded on the ship against loss or damage.
3. Freight insurance: the carrier insures the freight it would otherwise lose if the cargo is lost and the fee cannot be collected.

questions.stem_md: Three small pickle makers send 400, 350, 250 cartons to one warehouse, and a truck can carry 1,000. Name the warehousing function this shows, and explain two more functions of a warehouse.

questions.stem_md: Describe any three kinds of life insurance policy.
questions.solution_md: Any three kinds.

answer.model_answer_md:

2. Endowment policy: the sum is paid on death or on the end of a fixed term, whichever is earlier.
3. Annuity: the insurer makes regular payments to the insured for a period or for life. Joint life and children's policies are other kinds.

2. Cooperative banks are owned by members and serve farmers and small borrowers.

4. The central bank, the Reserve Bank of India, acts as banker to the government and to banks and regulates the system.

questions.stem_md: Explain any five principles of insurance, giving an imagined example of each.
questions.solution_md: Any five principles, each with an example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Utmost good faith: Kamlesh must disclose a heart ailment when buying a policy.
2. Insurable interest: a shop owner may insure her shop, but a stranger may not.
3. Indemnity: a loss of Rs 3,50,000 on a policy for Rs 5,00,000 brings a payment of Rs 3,50,000 only.
4. Proximate cause: a policy against fire does not cover a flood.
5. Subrogation: after paying, the insurer recovers from the careless contractor who caused the loss.

marking_scheme.step: Subrogation, contribution or mitigation with example

questions.stem_md: Distinguish among life, fire and marine insurance on any five points.
questions.solution_md: Five points of difference.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Nature: life insurance is a contract of guarantee; fire and marine insurance are contracts of indemnity.
2. Insurable interest: needed at the time of the contract in life insurance; at the time of contract and loss in fire insurance; at the time of loss in marine insurance.
3. Subject matter: a person's life, buildings and stock, and ships, cargo and freight respectively.
4. Compensation: fixed sum in life insurance; actual loss up to the sum insured in the others.
5. Cause: fire must be the proximate cause in fire insurance.

marking_scheme.step: Cause of loss or another valid point

questions.stem_md: Explain the functions of a warehouse.
questions.solution_md: Five functions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Consolidation: small lots from many sellers are joined into full loads.
2. Break-bulk: a large lot is split into small orders for retailers.
3. Stockpiling: goods are held until they are needed, especially seasonal goods.
4. Value-added services: grading, packing and labelling are done on the premises.
5. Price stabilisation and financing: stock is released to steady prices, and the receipt is accepted as security for a loan.
